title: Bowel (colon) cancer screening
question_forms: When should I start screening for colon or breast cancer?
When should Black people start bowel or colon cancer screening?
What is the bowel screening test (FIT)?
Should I get a colonoscopy before 50?
tradition_says: Bowel problems are often seen as embarrassing and put off, and some people think screening is only for people with symptoms or family history.

layer1.plain_answer: In England the NHS posts a home stool test every 2 years from 50 to 74; US guidance starts at 45. Screening works in the general population, and I found no trial of an earlier start for Black adults. Do the test when it arrives, and see a GP about blood in your poo.

do.text: Do the home FIT test when it arrives: the UK's NHS offers it to people aged 50 to 74 every 2 years, and over-74s can request a kit on 0800 707 6060.
See a doctor about bowel symptoms you are worried about, whether or not you have had screening.
If you are in the US, screening from 45 to 49 is recommended (a B recommendation) and from 50 to 75 is strongly recommended (an A recommendation).

avoid.text: Waiting for a screening invitation when you have symptoms: tell a doctor.
Assuming screening is only for older people: in the US about one in ten new cases is in people under 50, and cases in 40 to 49 year olds are rising.

see_someone_when: Blood in your poo, or a change in your bowel habit that lasts for weeks (doctor).
You are 50 or over and have not received a screening kit (your doctor's surgery or the national helpline).
A close relative had bowel cancer, especially before 50 (doctor: family history can change when screening should start; not covered here).

tested.population: Asymptomatic adults aged 45 or over at average risk, US; the review also examined whether findings varied by age, sex or race/ethnicity
tested.design: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement based on a commissioned systematic review and modelling
tested.finding: High certainty that screening aged 50 to 75 has substantial net benefit; moderate certainty that screening at 45 to 49 has moderate net benefit. About 10.5% of new US colorectal cancers are in people under 50, and incidence in 40 to 49 year olds rose by almost 15% between 2000-2002 and 2014-2016. The abstract does not report results by race.

source.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force, Davidson KW, Barry MJ, Mangione CM et al

tested.note: General US population, not Black-specific; the abstract states the review looked at race/ethnicity but gives no result.

tested.design: American Cancer Society statistics report from registries and death data
tested.finding: In 2023 about 153,020 people in the US would be diagnosed and 52,550 would die; incidence is rising 1-2% a year in people under 55, and 60% of new cases were advanced in 2019. The abstract names mortality rising in Native Americans, not Black people, and gives no Black-specific rate.

source.authors: Siegel RL, Wagle NS, Cercek A, Smith RA et al
source.journal: CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians

tested.note: Opened for Black-specific figures and found none in the abstract; the full report was not read.

tested.population: Earlier bowel screening for Black adults
tested.design: PubMed searches 12 Nov 2026: (colorectal cancer screening) AND (Black OR African American) AND (age 45 OR earlier screening OR incidence) restricted to systematic reviews and meta-analyses, 25 hits, titles read, none a review of an earlier start age for Black adults; (colorectal cancer) AND (Black OR African American) AND (early-onset OR younger than 50 OR age 45) AND incidence, 147 hits, first seven titles read, none a screening trial. Bowel screening uptake by ethnicity in England was not opened (49 records found). Positive control: the autism and burnout searches this session returned records.
tested.finding: My search found nothing: no trial or opened review testing whether Black adults should start bowel screening earlier than other adults.

tier_driver: That bowel screening reduces harm: a US task force rating of high certainty (50 to 75) and moderate certainty (45 to 49), in a general population. For Black adults specifically, I opened no evidence.
tier_note: B trial-other-population: the screening benefit is established in mixed populations; no Black-specific result was in the abstracts I opened. Moderate not strong, because the question for this site (should Black adults start earlier) is untested in what I read. NHS ages come from the NHS page opened today.
harm_note: No harm signal for taking the FIT test; colonoscopy after a positive test carries small procedure risks that I did not search.
evidence_summary: The NHS in England offers a home FIT test every 2 years to people aged 50 to 74 and tells everyone to see a GP about worrying bowel symptoms whether or not they have been screened; the page does not mention ethnicity. The US Preventive Services Task Force (2021) rates screening from 50 to 75 as high-certainty substantial net benefit and 45 to 49 as moderate-certainty moderate net benefit, and notes under-50 cases are rising. American Cancer Society statistics (2023) show the same younger shift but the abstract gives no Black-specific figures. My search found no trial or opened review of an earlier start for Black adults.
gaps: Untested or not opened: bowel cancer incidence, stage and death rates in Black adults in England and the US (the ACS report holds them; I read the abstract only); screening uptake by ethnic group in England (49 PubMed records found, none opened); whether Black adults gain more from starting at 45; colonoscopy access. NHS breast and bowel ages also sit in the breast and cancer screening entry.

sources.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force et al
